transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well… honestly, I’m here because I lost my temper in a way that really bothered me. I was on a board call, and somebody asked what should’ve been a pretty small, routine question about the facility budget — the kind of thing I answer all the time — and I just snapped.

I mean, I got sharp with them, more than sharp, really. It was out of proportion. That’s not how I run my company, and it’s not how I treat people. I’ve spent my whole career keeping control in meetings, especially with the board, so for me to react like that over a budget question… it made me think something’s not right, and I figured I should come talk to someone before it happens again.
Have you noticed yourself becoming unusually irritable or having trouble controlling your emotions in other situations recently?

Yes… that’s the thing that scared me. I’m not someone who usually loses control like that, especially not in a work setting. I mean, I’ve had plenty of tough calls, hard questions, budget fights, people pushing back on decisions — that comes with running a company. But this was just a small question about the facility budget, the kind of question that should’ve been nothing.

And I snapped. I got sharp, too sharp, in front of people I work with and answer to. It was out of proportion, and I knew it almost as soon as it came out of my mouth. That’s not how I run my company, and it’s not how I treat people. So yes, I’d say I’ve been having trouble keeping that irritation contained, at least in that moment, and it bothered me enough that I came here.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, outside of these moments of irritability?

Yes… not hopeless exactly, I don’t think, but definitely flat. That’s probably the best word for it.

There are a few things that usually settle me when I’m wound up — I’ll sit with a chess problem for a while, or look over my hiking notes, little route plans and observations I’ve made, that sort of thing. Or just having dinner with my wife, which normally helps me feel like I’m back in my own life and not just in work mode. Lately those things are there, and I go through the motions, but they don’t really reach me.

It’s strange, because I know intellectually that I should enjoy them. I’ll be sitting there with a chess position in front of me and I can recognize, “This is the kind of problem I usually like.” Or we’ll be at dinner and I know I should feel grateful and relaxed. But emotionally it’s just… muted. Like there’s a pane of glass between me and the feeling I’m supposed to have. I can see it, but I can’t quite get to it.
Have you found that you no longer take pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like chess or hiking?

Yes. I mean, I still do them, or I try to. It’s not like I’ve thrown the chessboard out or stopped looking at my hiking notes altogether. But the pleasure part of it feels… missing, or dulled.

A chess problem is usually something that pulls me in. I can sit there and turn it over in my head, and there’s usually a little satisfaction in seeing the pattern or finding the move. Lately I look at it and I know, in my head, “This is something I normally enjoy,” but I don’t feel that little spark from it.

Same with the hiking notes. I’ll look at routes or observations I wrote down, and normally that settles me, gives me something calm to focus on. Right now it just feels flat. Even dinner with my wife — which should be simple and grounding — I’m there, I’m participating, but it doesn’t quite reach me emotionally. It’s like I can recognize that I should be enjoying it, but I can’t quite get to the feeling.
When did you first start feeling this way — when did the flatness and loss of enjoyment begin?

It started right after the explosion and the fire during that walkthrough. Not months ago or anything like that — this has been going on about six days.

I remember feeling different almost immediately afterward, but the flatness became really noticeable over the next day or so. It’s like I came home and tried to fall back into my normal routines, the things that usually steady me, and they just didn’t work the way they’re supposed to. So… yes, about six days, since that incident.
Can you tell me more about the explosion and fire during the walkthrough — was it something that happened at work, and how were you involved?

I’m not sure how much detail you want there. I mean, yes, it was during a walkthrough, but I don’t know that I can lay it out cleanly like a report. I keep finding myself going back over little pieces of it and then losing the thread.

It was connected to work, yes — that’s the setting I associate it with. A walkthrough, people moving through, looking things over, and then suddenly it wasn’t normal anymore. There was the explosion and then the fire, and everything changed very fast. I don’t want to overstate my role because I’m not sure I have the whole sequence straight in my head. I was there, involved in the sense that I was part of the walkthrough and present when it happened.

That’s about as clearly as I can say it right now. It wasn’t something I heard about afterward or saw on the news. I was there when it happened.
Have you been feeling this way — flat and unable to enjoy things — every day or nearly every day for at least two weeks?

No, not two weeks. It feels like it’s been longer because the days have been sort of stretched out and strange, but if I’m being accurate, it’s been about six days.

It started after the explosion and fire during the walkthrough. Since then, each day I’ve noticed that flat feeling — like the things I normally enjoy just don’t land the same way. But it has not been two weeks. It’s been less than that, about six days.
Since the explosion and fire, have you had flashbacks, nightmares, or found yourself avoiding reminders of what happened?

Yes… I mean, I don’t know if I’d call them flashbacks exactly, but something like that happens. I’ll be in the middle of a call, trying to listen to somebody talk through something ordinary, or I’ll be looking at numbers on a page — just regular work stuff — and then it just jumps back into my head.

It’s the blast, and that fire by the loading area. It comes in like a bad film I didn’t ask to see, if that makes sense. Not like I’m choosing to think about it or sitting there replaying it on purpose. It just sort of cuts in, and for a moment that’s what’s in front of me instead of the call or the numbers.

I haven’t really known what to do with that, because I’m used to being able to focus and keep things moving, and this feels… intrusive, I guess. It catches me off guard.
